claim: Flaviviruses include numerous important human pathogens, e.g., dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV).
source: Flaviviruses include numerous important human pathogens, e.g., dengue virus (DENV) and Zika virus (ZIKV).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about flaviviruses and their importance as human pathogens.

claim: A highly conserved, conformation-tunable cis-acting element named 5′-UAR-flanking stem (UFS) exists in the flavivirus genomic 5′ terminus.
source: Here, we revealed a highly conserved, conformation-tunable cis-acting element named 5′-UAR-flanking stem (UFS) in the flavivirus genomic 5′ terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bioinformatics analysis, SHAPE data, and structural predictions presented in the manuscript.

claim: The UFS is critical for efficient NS5 recruitment and viral RNA synthesis in different flaviviruses.
source: We demonstrated that the UFS was critical for efficient NS5 recruitment and viral RNA synthesis in different flaviviruses.
evidence: This is supported by EMSA assays showing NS5Pol binding (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), RdRp activity assays (Figure 6D), and replicon assays (Figure 3D, Figure 7B).

claim: Stabilization of the DENV UFS impaired both genome cyclization and vRNA replication.
source: Interestingly, stabilization of the DENV UFS impaired both genome cyclization and vRNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by replicon assays showing reduced replication of over-stabilized UFS mutants (Figure 7B) and RNA binding assays showing impaired 5′-3′ interactions (Figure 8B).

claim: The UFS unwinds in response to genome cyclization, leading to decreased affinity of NS5 for the viral 5′ end.
source: Moreover, the UFS unwound in response to genome cyclization, leading to the decreased affinity of NS5 for the viral 5′ end.
evidence: This is supported by SHAPE analysis showing increased reactivity of UFS region in presence of 3′ UTR (Figure 9), and EMSA showing reduced NS5Pol binding to circularized mini-genomes (Figure 10C).

claim: The UFS is switched by genome cyclization to regulate dynamic RdRp binding for vRNA replication.
source: Thus, we propose that the UFS is switched by genome cyclization to regulate dynamic RdRp binding for vRNA replication.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the combined data from SHAPE, EMSA, RdRp assays, and replicon experiments.

claim: The UFS enables communication between flavivirus genome cyclization and RdRp recruitment.
source: This study demonstrates that the UFS enables communication between flavivirus genome cyclization and RdRp recruitment, highlighting the presence of switch-like mechanisms among RNA viruses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing the UFS responds to genome cyclization and affects NS5 binding.

claim: Cis-acting regulatory elements play essential yet diverse roles in the life cycle of RNA viruses.
source: Cis-acting regulatory elements play essential yet diverse roles in the life cycle of RNA viruses (Liu et al., 2009; Nicholson and White, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cis-acting elements have been found to regulate viral replicase binding and viral RNA synthesis.
source: These elements have been found to regulate viral replicase binding and viral RNA (vRNA) synthesis (Filomatori et al., 2006; Vogt and Andino, 2010; Wu et al., 2009), nucleocapsid assembly (Goto et al., 2013; Keane et al., 2015; Morales et al., 2013), and viral translation (Brierley and Dos Ramos, 2006; Kieft, 2008; Liu et al., 2009; Simon and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Local RNA elements in viral genomes are often involved in long-range RNA-RNA interactions.
source: In particular, local RNA elements in viral genomes are often involved in long-range RNA-RNA interactions (Alvarez et al., 2005; Nicholson and White, 2014; Shetty et al., 2013), which are often referred to as genome cyclization and can bring regions separated by several thousand nucleotides into proximity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The genus flavivirus includes important causative agents for human diseases, such as dengue virus (DENV1-4), West Nile virus (WNV), Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), yellow fever virus (YFV) and the emerging Zika virus (ZIKV).
source: The genus flavivirus includes important causative agents for human diseases, such as dengue virus (DENV1-4), West Nile virus (WNV), Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), yellow fever virus (YFV) and the emerging Zika virus (ZIKV) (Fauci and Morens, 2016; Mlakar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Major phylogenetic groups of flaviviruses include mosquito-borne flaviviruses (MBFVs), tick-borne flaviviruses (TBFVs), insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFVs) and flaviviruses with no known vectors (NKVs).
source: Major phylogenetic groups (Blitvich and Firth, 2015; Moureau et al., 2015) of flaviviruses include mosquito-borne flaviviruses (MBFVs), tick-borne flaviviruses (TBFVs), insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFVs) and flaviviruses with no known vectors (NKVs).
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The flavivirus genome is approximately 11 kb and contains a single ORF, which encodes a polyprotein precursor with more than 3000 residues.
source: The flaviviruses are single-stranded, positive-sense RNA viruses, and their genome is approximately 11 kb and contains a single ORF, which encodes a polyprotein precursor with more than 3000 residues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus genome organization.

claim: The flavivirus polyprotein precursor is processed into 3 structural proteins (capsid, pre-membrane/membrane and envelope) and at least 7 nonstructural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B and NS5).
source: The precursor is further processed into 3 structural proteins (capsid, pre-membrane/membrane and envelope) and at least 7 nonstructural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B and NS5).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus protein processing.

claim: NS5 performs methyltransferase, guanylyltransferase and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) activity.
source: The largest nonstructural protein, NS5, performs methyltransferase (Egloff et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2007), guanylyltransferase (Issur et al., 2009) and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) activity (Nomaguchi et al., 2003; Uchil and Satchidanandam, 2003; Yap et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NS5 interacts with vRNA, other viral nonstructural proteins and host factors to assemble to the viral replication complex essential for vRNA synthesis.
source: NS5 interacts with vRNA, other viral nonstructural proteins and host factors to assemble to the viral replication complex essential for vRNA synthesis (Klema et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The highly structured 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) occupy the termini of the flavivirus genome.
source: On the other hand, the highly structured 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs) occupy the termini of the viral genome (Friebe and Harris, 2010; Gebhard et al., 2011; Villordo et al., 2016) and contain cis-acting elements crucial for vRNA replication (Clyde et al., 2008; Filomatori et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013; Lodeiro et al., 2009; Rouha et al., 2011; Villordo et al., 2010), translation (Chiu et al., 2005; Clyde and Harris, 2006), viral pathogenesis (Chapman et al., 2014; Funk et al., 2010; Roby et al., 2014) and host adaptation (Villordo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hybridization of complementary sequences at the 5′ and 3′ termini, which include the 5′-3′ upstream AUG region (UAR), downstream AUG region (DAR) and cyclization sequence (CS) elements, circularizes the genome of MBFV.
source: Hybridization of complementary sequences at the 5′ and 3′ termini, which include the 5′-3′ upstream AUG region (UAR) (Alvarez et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2008), downstream AUG region (DAR) (Friebe and Harris, 2010; Friebe et al., 2011) and cyclization sequence (CS) (Khromykh et al., 2001) elements, circularizes the genome of MBFV.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Genome cyclization is modulated by the downstream of 5′ CS pseudoknot (DCS-PK) in the capsid-coding region.
source: Genome cyclization, which is also modulated by the downstream of 5′ CS pseudoknot (DCS-PK) in the capsid-coding region (de Borba et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013), is crucial for the translocation of NS5 from the 5′ stem-loop A (SLA) promoter to the RNA synthesis initiation site at the 3′ end (Filomatori et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Genome cyclization is crucial for the translocation of NS5 from the 5′ stem-loop A (SLA) promoter to the RNA synthesis initiation site at the 3′ end.
source: Genome cyclization, which is also modulated by the downstream of 5′ CS pseudoknot (DCS-PK) in the capsid-coding region (de Borba et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2013), is crucial for the translocation of NS5 from the 5′ stem-loop A (SLA) promoter to the RNA synthesis initiation site at the 3′ end (Filomatori et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The 5′ SLA structure and genome cyclization strategy were identified in other phylogenetic groups of the flavivirus genus, although the specific details differ.
source: The 5′ SLA structure and genome cyclization strategy were also identified in other phylogenetic groups of the flavivirus genus, although the specific details differ.
evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatics analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 1 and Figure 12.

claim: The 5′ UAR element in MBFV usually participates in the formation of a local hairpin, stem-loop B (SLB), in the linear conformation of the vRNA.
source: The 5′ UAR element in MBFV usually participates in the formation of a local hairpin, stem-loop B (SLB), in the linear conformation of the vRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MBFV RNA structure.

claim: The SLA and SLB elements are separated by a short uracil-rich sequence, which has been shown to mediate vRNA replication of DENV.
source: The SLA and SLB elements are separated by a short uracil-rich sequence, which has been shown to mediate vRNA replication of DENV (Lodeiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The U-rich region of MBFV is involved in the formation of a conserved RNA duplex designated as a 5′-UAR-flanking stem (UFS).
source: In the present study, we demonstrated that the U-rich region of MBFV is involved in the formation of a conserved RNA duplex that is designated as a 5′-UAR-flanking stem (UFS) because it locks the 5′ UAR/SLB element between its two strands.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis (Figure 1) and SHAPE data (Figure 2).

claim: The UFS locks the 5′ UAR/SLB element between its two strands.
source: In the present study, we demonstrated that the U-rich region of MBFV is involved in the formation of a conserved RNA duplex that is designated as a 5′-UAR-flanking stem (UFS) because it locks the 5′ UAR/SLB element between its two strands.
evidence: This is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: UFS switching is a general replication strategy in flaviviruses with vertebrate hosts.
source: Furthermore, UFS switching is a general replication strategy in flaviviruses with vertebrate hosts, highlighting their role in the host adaptation and evolution of flaviviruses.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 12 demonstrating that 5′ local structures downstream of SLA are consistently melted during genome cyclization across different flavivirus groups.

claim: Representative sequences derived from various flavivirus species were subjected to the mfold RNA folding server for structure prediction.
source: To clarify the structural characteristics of the region downstream of SLA, representative sequences derived from various flavivirus species were subjected to the mfold RNA folding server (Zuker, 2003; Zuker and Jacobson, 1998).
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: Structure prediction showed that the U-rich region of most MBFVs (except the YFV clade) forms a duplex with complementary sequences in or near the viral translational starting region.
source: Structure prediction of the 5′ end local structures showed that the U-rich region of most MBFVs (except the YFV clade) forms a duplex with complementary sequences in or near the viral translational starting region (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the computational predictions shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The UFS duplex was predicted to unwind due to the formation of the panhandle structure between the 5′ and 3′ ends when long-range interactions between the genome termini were considered.
source: Furthermore, the UFS duplex was predicted to unwind due to the formation of the panhandle structure between the 5′ and 3′ ends when long-range interactions between the genome termini were considered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The UFS element has been identified in MBFVs, two clades of NKVs, and ISFVs.
source: Local structures similar to UFS were also identified in ISFVs (Figure 1B) and Modoc virus (MODV) among the NKVs (Figure 1B), whereas the non-vectored Rio Bravo virus (RBV, Figure 1B) was shown to contain a ψUFS structure.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparisons shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The UFS in MBFVs and UFS-like structures in NKVs are involved in genome cyclization.
source: The UFS and ψUFS in NKVs were also involved in genome cyclization, similar to the corresponding structures in MBFVs.
evidence: This is supported by the structural predictions and comparisons shown in Figure 1 and supplementary files.

claim: The UFS-like structures in ISFVs were not predicted to be involved in genome cyclization.
source: In contrast, the UFS-like structures were not predicted to be involved in genome cyclization in ISFVs, suggesting that the UFS in MBFVs and UFS-like structures in ISFVs function differently.
evidence: This is based on computational predictions and structural analysis.

claim: The UFS/ψUFS structure was not identified in TBFVs or in the Yokose virus clade of NKVs.
source: Finally, the UFS/ψUFS structure was not identified in TBFVs or in the Yokose virus clade of NKVs; instead, a short hairpin with a large loop occupied the analogous location of the UFS in these viruses (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The secondary structures of UFS elements are affected by genome conformation.
source: Taken together, the above results demonstrated the conservation of UFS elements among the flavivirus genus and suggested that the secondary structures of UFS elements are affected by genome conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the computational predictions showing UFS unwinding during genome cyclization.

claim: RNA molecules corresponding to the 5′ ends of DENV1-4, JEV and ZIKV were analyzed by SHAPE.
source: To investigate whether the duplex conformation of the UFS can indeed exist locally under in vitro conditions, RNA molecules corresponding to the 5′ ends of DENV1-4, JEV and ZIKV were analyzed by selective 2′-hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension (SHAPE).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The SHAPE results agreed well with the predicted RNA structures for JEV, DENV1, DENV3, DENV4, and ZIKV.
source: The SHAPE results were shown to agree well with the predicted RNA structures. It was shown that the UFS element of JEV forms a conical duplex structure under in vitro conditions (Figure 2A) because all nucleotides of the UFS exhibited low SHAPE reactivity. Similar results were obtained for DENV serotypes 1, 3, 4 and ZIKV (Figure 2B,D,E and F), except that several nucleotides in the ZIKV and DENV1/3 UFS regions had elevated SHAPE reactivity, which was likely due to the presence of internal loops.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The UFS duplex of DENV2 is highly unstable under in vitro conditions.
source: In contrast, the SHAPE results indicated that the UFS duplex of DENV2 is highly unstable because the DENV2 UFS region showed considerable SHAPE reactivity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of the DENV UFS duplex conformation was confirmed by SHAPE analysis of DENV3 5′ end RNA molecules containing mutations in the UFS.
source: The presence of the DENV UFS duplex conformation was further confirmed by SHAPE analysis of DENV3 5′ end RNA molecules containing mutations in the UFS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SHAPE reactivity of the UFS region significantly increased in UFS-disrupted mutants (D3-M13A and D3-M13B).
source: It was shown that the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS region significantly increased in UFS-disrupted mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, D3-M13A and D3-M13B), and restoration of UFS base-pairing endowed the corresponding region with low SHAPE reactivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, D3-M13C).
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Restoration of UFS base-pairing endowed the corresponding region with low SHAPE reactivity (D3-M13C).
source: It was shown that the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS region significantly increased in UFS-disrupted mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, D3-M13A and D3-M13B), and restoration of UFS base-pairing endowed the corresponding region with low SHAPE reactivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, D3-M13C).
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The UFS duplex can exist locally in the vRNA 5′ end under in vitro conditions.
source: The above results demonstrated that the UFS duplex can exist locally in the vRNA 5′ end under in vitro conditions, suggesting that the UFS can assume the duplex conformation, at least under certain states of the flavivirus genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the SHAPE data showing low reactivity in the UFS region.

claim: Functional mutagenesis of the UFS was performed using a DENV4 replicon with internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-controlled viral translation.
source: Functional mutagenesis of the UFS was performed using a DENV4 replicon with internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-controlled viral translation (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: Disrupting the base-pairing of the UFS (M1A, M1B, M3A and M3B) greatly reduced vRNA replication.
source: Disrupting the base-pairing of the UFS (Figure 3C,D. M1A, M1B, M3A and M3B) greatly reduced vRNA replication, whereas reconstituting base-pairing by combining the corresponding mutations was able to restore vRNA replication (Figure 3C,D. M1C and M3C), although the M3C mutant replicated moderately less efficiently than the wild-type (WT) replicon, possibly due to the apparent primary sequence changes in the U-rich region.
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Reconstituting UFS base-pairing by combining the corresponding mutations was able to restore vRNA replication (M1C and M3C).
source: Disrupting the base-pairing of the UFS (Figure 3C,D. M1A, M1B, M3A and M3B) greatly reduced vRNA replication, whereas reconstituting base-pairing by combining the corresponding mutations was able to restore vRNA replication (Figure 3C,D. M1C and M3C), although the M3C mutant replicated moderately less efficiently than the wild-type (WT) replicon, possibly due to the apparent primary sequence changes in the U-rich region.
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The overall genome cyclization pattern was only slightly affected by the M1 and M3 mutations.
source: Next, the impact of the M1 and M3 mutations on the circularized vRNA structure was assessed using the mfold online server. It was shown that the overall genome cyclization pattern was only slightly affected by the M1 and M3 mutations (Supplementary file 3), and the changes in the stability of the predicted circularized structures was considerable smaller than the changes in the local UFS structure.
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Disruption of UFS base pairing (mutant AGU and GAU) reduced vRNA replication greatly.
source: It was shown that disruption of UFS base pairing (mutant AGU and GAU) reduced vRNA replication greatly, whereas substituting of a few base pairs in the UFS (mutant AUA and ACG) only have moderate effects on vRNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substituting a few base pairs in the UFS (mutant AUA and ACG) only have moderate effects on vRNA replication.
source: It was shown that disruption of UFS base pairing (mutant AGU and GAU) reduced vRNA replication greatly, whereas substituting of a few base pairs in the UFS (mutant AUA and ACG) only have moderate effects on vRNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SHAPE analysis confirmed that the UFS structure was disrupted/destabilized or reconstituted as aimed by the M1A, M1C, M3A or M3C mutations.
source: To confirm that the RNA conformation was changed as expected by the corresponding mutations, SHAPE analysis was performed for DENV4 5′-300 nt RNA containing the M1A, M1C, M3A or M3C mutation, and the SHAPE results were compared with WT RNA (Figure 4). In WT RNA, nucleotides composing the UFS only showed low or background SHAPE reactivity, whereas the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS region increased significantly in the M1A and M3A mutants, suggesting that the UFS duplex was indeed disrupted by the corresponding mutations. In contrast, the M1C and M3C mutations greatly reduced the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS region.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RNA structure predictions using the RNAstructure software with SHAPE constraints confirmed that the UFS structure was disrupted/destabilized or reconstituted as aimed, and these mutations did not affect the overall secondary structure of the 5′ end RNA.
source: RNA structure predictions using the RNAstructure (Reuter and Mathews, 2010) software with SHAPE constraints confirmed that the UFS structure was disrupted/destabilized or reconstituted as aimed, and these mutations did not affect the overall secondary structure of the 5′ end RNA (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The presence of the UFS greatly enhances vRNA replication, and this function is directly correlated to its duplex conformation.
source: Taken together, the above results demonstrated that the presence of the UFS greatly enhances vRNA replication, and this function is directly correlated to its duplex conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined replicon and SHAPE data showing that disrupting the UFS duplex reduces replication while restoring it recovers replication.

claim: Various mutations targeting the UFS element were introduced into a DENV4 infectious clone.
source: We further attempted to investigate the influence of the UFS on the propagation of infectious virus. Various mutations targeting the UFS element (Figures 3 and 5A) were introduced into a DENV4 infectious clone.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: The vRNA copies in BHK-21 cells transfected with the M1A, M3A or M5A mutants were significantly lower than those transfected with WT vRNA at 48–72 hr post-transfection.
source: vRNA copies in BHK-21 cells were determined at different time points post-electroporation (Figure 5B–D). It was shown that the vRNA copies in BHK-21 cells transfected with the M1A, M3A or M5A mutants were significantly lower than those transfected with WT vRNA at 48–72 hr post-transfection, whereas restoration of the UFS element by complementary mutations partially (Figure 5C, M3C) or fully (Figure 5B,D. M1C and M5C) recovered the vRNA replication levels, highlighting the importance of the UFS for vRNA replication of infection-competent viruses.
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Restoration of the UFS element by complementary mutations partially (M3C) or fully (M1C and M5C) recovered the vRNA replication levels.
source: vRNA copies in BHK-21 cells were determined at different time points post-electroporation (Figure 5B–D). It was shown that the vRNA copies in BHK-21 cells transfected with the M1A, M3A or M5A mutants were significantly lower than those transfected with WT vRNA at 48–72 hr post-transfection, whereas restoration of the UFS element by complementary mutations partially (Figure 5C, M3C) or fully (Figure 5B,D. M1C and M5C) recovered the vRNA replication levels, highlighting the importance of the UFS for vRNA replication of infection-competent viruses.
evidence: This is supported by the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The DENV-positive rates were apparently lower in cells transfected with UFS-disrupted mutants than in those transfected with UFS-restored mutants or WT vRNA at the same time points.
source: An indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA, Figure 5E) revealed that the DENV-positive rates were apparently lower in cells transfected with UFS-disrupted mutants than in those transfected with UFS-restored mutants or WT vRNA at the same time points.
evidence: This is supported by the IFA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The virus titers in the culture supernatants of M1A-transfected BHK-21 cells were significantly lower than those of M1C- or WT-transfected cells.
source: The virus titers in the culture supernatants of M1A-transfected BHK-21 cells were also significantly lower than those of M1C- or WT-transfected cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the virus titration data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Only negligible differences in RNA stability were found between WT RNA and the mutants of the M1 or M3 groups.
source: The effect of UFS mutations on vRNA stability was then assessed. To this end, DENV4 NS5-GVD-vRNAs containing different UFS mutations were transfected into BHK-21 cells by electroporation, and vRNA copies were determined at 4, 24, 48 and 72 hr post-transfection. Only negligible differences in RNA stability were found between WT RNA and the mutants of the M1 or M3 groups (Figure 5G,H), and the stability of the M5C mutant was moderately reduced compared with that of the M5A mutant (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA stability data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The differences in the RNA stability of the UFS mutants did not account for their different replication characteristics.
source: Thus, the differences in the RNA stability of the UFS mutants did not account for their different replication characteristics.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA stability data showing minimal differences between mutants.

claim: The UFS element is required for virus propagation due to its function in vRNA replication.
source: The above results demonstrated that the UFS element is required for virus propagation due to its function in vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing reduced viral propagation in UFS-disrupted mutants.

claim: Disrupting of the UFS greatly reduced viral propagation of ZIKV, whereas reconstitution of the UFS duplex restores ZIKV propagation.
source: In agreement with the function of DENV4 UFS, we also showed that disrupting of the UFS greatly reduced viral propagation of ZIKV, whereas reconstitution of the UFS duplex restores ZIKV propagation by IFA tests performed in transfected BHK-21 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the IFA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT and UFS-mutated DENV4 5′-300 nt RNA molecules were incubated with different concentrations of the NS5 RdRp domain (NS5Pol), and the reaction mixtures were analyzed by native PAGE.
source: WT and UFS-mutated DENV4 5′-300 nt RNA molecules were incubated with different concentrations of the NS5 RdRp domain (NS5Pol), and the reaction mixtures were analyzed by native PAGE.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The binding of NS5Pol to 5′-300 nt RNA containing the M1A or M1B mutation in UFS was much weaker than the binding to 5′-300 nt WT RNA.
source: The binding of NS5Pol to 5′-300 nt RNA containing the M1A or M1B mutation in UFS was much weaker than the binding to 5′-300 nt WT RNA, whereas the 5′-300 nt M1C and WT RNA bound to NS5Pol with comparable affinity (Figure 6C, top and middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 5′-300 nt M1C and WT RNA bound to NS5Pol with comparable affinity.
source: The binding of NS5Pol to 5′-300 nt RNA containing the M1A or M1B mutation in UFS was much weaker than the binding to 5′-300 nt WT RNA, whereas the 5′-300 nt M1C and WT RNA bound to NS5Pol with comparable affinity (Figure 6C, top and middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 5′-300 nt M3A and M3B RNA interacted with NS5Pol weakly, whereas the combination of the two mutations apparently restored the interaction between NS5Pol and 5′-300 nt M3C RNA.
source: The 5′-300 nt M3A and M3B RNA also interacted with NS5Pol weakly, whereas the combination of the two mutations apparently restored the interaction between NS5Pol and 5′-300 nt M3C RNA (Figure 6C, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The UFS duplex is required for efficient NS5Pol binding in DENV4.
source: The above results indicated that the UFS duplex is required for efficient NS5Pol binding in DENV4.
evidence: This is inferred from the EMSA data showing reduced binding for UFS-disrupted mutants.

claim: The UFS duplex is important for the efficient binding of JEV NS5Pol to its 5′ end RNA.
source: Moreover, EMSA assay demonstrated that the UFS duplex is also important for the efficient binding of JEV NS5Pol to its 5′ end RNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the function of UFS in viral RdRp recruitment is conserved among flaviviruses.
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The function of UFS in viral RdRp recruitment is conserved among flaviviruses.
source: Moreover, EMSA assay demonstrated that the UFS duplex is also important for the efficient binding of JEV NS5Pol to its 5′ end RNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the function of UFS in viral RdRp recruitment is conserved among flaviviruses.
evidence: This is inferred from the EMSA data showing similar effects in both DENV4 and JEV.

claim: Apparently fewer RdRp products were generated in the reactions containing templates with disrupted UFS elements compared with the reaction containing the 5′-160 nt WT template.
source: Next, in vitro RdRp assays using DENV4 5′-160 nt RNA as a template were performed to investigate whether the role of the UFS in NS5Pol recruitment is required for de novo RNA synthesis (Figure 6D). Apparently fewer products were generated in the reactions containing templates with disrupted UFS elements compared with the reaction containing the 5′-160 nt WT template, and restoration of the UFS duplex greatly increased the amounts of RdRp products in reactions using the corresponding 5′-160 nt mutants as templates.
evidence: This is supported by the RdRp assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Restoration of the UFS duplex greatly increased the amounts of RdRp products in reactions using the corresponding 5′-160 nt mutants as templates.
source: Next, in vitro RdRp assays using DENV4 5′-160 nt RNA as a template were performed to investigate whether the role of the UFS in NS5Pol recruitment is required for de novo RNA synthesis (Figure 6D). Apparently fewer products were generated in the reactions containing templates with disrupted UFS elements compared with the reaction containing the 5′-160 nt WT template, and restoration of the UFS duplex greatly increased the amounts of RdRp products in reactions using the corresponding 5′-160 nt mutants as templates.
evidence: This is supported by the RdRp assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: An EMSA experiment using 5′-160 nt RNA as a probe confirmed the function of UFS in NS5Pol recruitment, although the overall affinity of 5′-160 nt RNA for NS5Pol was lower than that of 5′-300 nt RNA.
source: Moreover, an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) experiment using 5′-160 nt RNA as a probe confirmed the function of UFS in NS5Pol recruitment, although the overall affinity of 5′-160 nt RNA for NS5Pol was lower than that of 5′-300 nt RNA (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The duplex conformation of the UFS element is required for efficient NS5 recruitment and de novo initiation efficiency, which is closely correlated with its function in vRNA replication.
source: Taken together, the above results demonstrated that the duplex conformation of the UFS element is required for efficient NS5 recruitment and de novo initiation efficiency, which is closely correlated with its function in vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined EMSA and RdRp assay data.

claim: UA base pairs of the DENV4 UFS were progressively substituted with GC base pairs to investigate whether the low stability of the UFS duplex is associated with its function.
source: The UFS elements were shown to be rich in UA/AU base pairs, which contribute less to the stability of RNA structures than CG/GC base pairs. Furthermore, internal loops and/or wobble base pairs are prevalent inside the UFS or at the junction connecting the UFS and SLB, which further decreases their structural stability. To investigate whether the low stability of the UFS duplex is associated with its function, UA base pairs of the DENV4 UFS were progressively substituted with GC base pairs, and the replication efficiency of the corresponding mutants was assessed using the above replicon system in BHK-21 cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: All mutants containing disrupted UFS elements showed only extremely low levels of replication (M2A, M2B, M4A and M4B).
source: As expected, all mutants containing disrupted UFS elements showed only extremely low levels of replication (Figure 7, M2A, M2B, M4A and M4B).
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: One single UA-to-GC substitution at different positions (M2C1 and M2C2) had little effect on vRNA replication.
source: One single UA-to-GC substitution at different positions (Figure 7, M2C1 and M2C2) had little effect on vRNA replication, in agreement with the above results (Figure 3, M1C).
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: All UFS mutants containing 2 or more UA-to-GC base pair substitutions replicated poorly compared with the WT replicon (M2C and M4C).
source: Surprisingly, all UFS mutants containing 2 or more UA-to-GC base pair substitutions replicated poorly compared with the WT replicon (Figure 7, M2C and M4C).
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Increasing the stability of the UFS duplex is harmful for vRNA replication.
source: The above results indicated that increasing the stability of the UFS duplex is harmful for vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the replicon data showing reduced replication for over-stabilized UFS mutants.

claim: Shortening the length of the internal loop between UFS and SLB to 1 nt or 2 nt did not affect vRNA replication greatly.
source: To further confirm this finding and rule out the possibility that the base pair composition itself affects UFS function, another panel of replicon mutants, which targeted the 3-nt internal loop region between the DENV4 UFS and SLB, was generated. Shortening the length of the internal loop to 1 nt or 2 nt did not affect vRNA replication greatly.
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total deletion of the internal loop between UFS and SLB, which caused the SLB to stack onto the UFS, significantly reduced the vRNA replication efficiency (L1D, L2D and L3D).
source: In contrast, total deletion of the internal loop, which caused the SLB to stack onto the UFS, significantly reduced the vRNA replication efficiency (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, L1D, L2D and L3D).
evidence: This is supported by the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The purine-rich properties of the internal loop are optimal for efficient DENV4 vRNA replication.
source: Moreover, replication assays performed for various purine-to-purine and purine-to-pyrimidine substituting mutations targeting the internal loop (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggested that the purine-rich properties of the internal loop are optimal for efficient DENV4 vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the replicon assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stability of the UFS duplex is a critical determinant for its function in vRNA replication.
source: Taken together, the above results demonstrated that the stability of the UFS duplex is a critical determinant for its function in vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined replicon data showing optimal replication requires balanced UFS stability.

claim: The defects in the vRNA replication of the over-stabilized UFS mutants were not caused by alternations in their affinity for NS5Pol.
source: The defects in the vRNA replication of the over-stabilized UFS mutants were not caused by alternations in their affinity for NS5Pol, as an EMSA indicated that the 5′-300 nt M2C RNA bound to NS5Pol efficiently (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNA structure prediction and a previous report suggested that the UFS duplex is melted after genome cyclization.
source: RNA structure prediction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1) and a previous report (Sztuba-Solinska et al., 2013) suggested that the UFS duplex is melted after genome cyclization, whereas the 5′ UAR/SLB element, which is locked by the UFS duplex, is important for flavivirus genome cyclization (Alvarez et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by computational predictions and citations to previous literature.

claim: The 5′ UAR/SLB element, which is locked by the UFS duplex, is important for flavivirus genome cyclization.
source: RNA structure prediction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1) and a previous report (Sztuba-Solinska et al., 2013) suggested that the UFS duplex is melted after genome cyclization, whereas the 5′ UAR/SLB element, which is locked by the UFS duplex, is important for flavivirus genome cyclization (Alvarez et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The M1A, M1B and M1C mutations had little effect on the formation of 5′-3′ complex.
source: The M1A, M1B and M1C mutations (Figure 8B), as well as the M3 series mutations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), had little effect on the formation of 5′-3′ complex.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA binding assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The M3 series mutations had little effect on the formation of 5′-3′ complex.
source: The M1A, M1B and M1C mutations (Figure 8B), as well as the M3 series mutations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), had little effect on the formation of 5′-3′ complex.
evidence: This is supported by the RNA binding assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The M2A and M2B mutations did not influence the formation of 5′-3′ RNA complex apparently.
source: However, when the M2 series mutants were assayed, although the M2A and M2B mutations also did not influence the formation of 5′-3′ RNA complex apparently, the complex formed by the 3′ UTR and 5′-300 nt M2C RNA was greatly reduced compared to the amounts of complexes formed by the 3′ UTR and other 5′-300 nt RNA species (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA binding assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The complex formed by the 3′ UTR and 5′-300 nt M2C RNA was greatly reduced compared to the amounts of complexes formed by the 3′ UTR and other 5′-300 nt RNA species.
source: However, when the M2 series mutants were assayed, although the M2A and M2B mutations also did not influence the formation of 5′-3′ RNA complex apparently, the complex formed by the 3′ UTR and 5′-300 nt M2C RNA was greatly reduced compared to the amounts of complexes formed by the 3′ UTR and other 5′-300 nt RNA species (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA binding assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The Kd of 5′-300 nt M2C binding with 3′ UTR is approximately ten fold higher than the Kds of the other 5′ RNAs.
source: Estimation of dissociation constant (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) revealed that the Kd of 5′-300 nt M2C binding with 3′ UTR is approximately ten fold higher than the Kds of the other 5′ RNAs.
evidence: This is supported by the Kd estimation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing the stability of the UFS hinders vRNA terminus interactions.
source: These results together indicated that increasing the stability of the UFS hinders vRNA terminus interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA binding assay data showing reduced 5′-3′ complex formation for M2C.

claim: The 5′-300 nt L3D mutant, in which the internal loop was deleted, also interacted with the 3′ UTR poorly.
source: Furthermore, the 5′-300 nt L3D mutant, in which the internal loop was deleted, also interacted with the 3′ UTR poorly (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA binding assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the 5′:3′ ratio was 1:1, the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS element in 5′-300 nt WT RNA exhibited a significant increase compared with the reactivity when the 3′ UTR was absent.
source: SHAPE analysis was then performed to observe the structural changes to 5′ end RNA caused by different concentrations of 3′ UTR RNA (Figure 9). When the 5′:3′ ratio was 1:1, the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS element in 5′-300 nt WT RNA exhibited a significant increase compared with the reactivity when the 3′ UTR was absent, and the SHAPE reactivity of the SLB loop and 5′ CS region was obviously reduced.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the 3′ UTR was in 5-fold excess of 5′-300 nt RNA, the SLB loop region of WT 5′ RNA showed essentially no SHAPE reactivity, indicating a complete transition from the SLB structure to a UAR duplex.
source: When the 3′ UTR was in 5-fold excess of 5′-300 nt RNA, the SLB loop region of WT 5′ RNA showed essentially no SHAPE reactivity, indicating a complete transition from the SLB structure to a UAR duplex.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the 5′-300 nt M2C RNA was incubated with an equal concentration of 3′ UTR RNA, there were only minor changes in the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS and SLB loop regions compared with those of 5′-300 nt M2C RNA alone.
source: In contrast, when the 5′-300 nt M2C RNA was incubated with an equal concentration of 3′ UTR RNA, there were only minor changes in the SHAPE reactivity of the UFS and SLB loop regions compared with those of 5′-300 nt M2C RNA alone.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the 5′:3′ ratio was 1:5, the SLB loop region of 5′-300 nt M2C RNA still showed moderate SHAPE reactivity.
source: When the 5′:3′ ratio was 1:5, the SLB loop region of 5′-300 nt M2C RNA still showed moderate SHAPE reactivity.
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The UFS duplex is melted when the 3′ UTR binds to 5′ end RNA.
source: The above results demonstrated that the UFS duplex is melted when the 3′ UTR binds to 5′ end RNA, and stabilization of the UFS renders it difficult to unwind in response to the 3′ UTR and thus hinders genome cyclization.
evidence: This is inferred from the SHAPE data showing increased UFS reactivity in presence of 3′ UTR.

claim: Stabilization of the UFS renders it difficult to unwind in response to the 3′ UTR and thus hinders genome cyclization.
source: The above results demonstrated that the UFS duplex is melted when the 3′ UTR binds to 5′ end RNA, and stabilization of the UFS renders it difficult to unwind in response to the 3′ UTR and thus hinders genome cyclization.
evidence: This is inferred from the SHAPE data showing M2C resists unwinding in presence of 3′ UTR.

claim: The stability of the UFS secondary structure must be maintained below a threshold to enable the necessary conformational changes required for genome cyclization.
source: Thus, although the UFS does not participate in 5′-3′ hybridization directly, the stability of its secondary structure must be maintained below a threshold to enable the necessary conformational changes required for genome cyclization.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing over-stabilized UFS impairs genome cyclization.

claim: The unwinding of the UFS during genome cyclization may be important for its function in viral RNA synthesis.
source: It can be speculated that the unwinding of the UFS during genome cyclization may be important for its function in viral RNA synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed correlation between UFS unwinding and genome cyclization.

claim: The DENV4 WT mini-genome, as well as the M1A, M1B, M1C, M3A, M3B, M3C and M2A mini-genomes, existed mostly in a circularized conformation.
source: First, using native PAGE, we found that the WT mini-genome, as well as the M1A, M1B, M1C, M3A, M3B, M3C and M2A mini-genomes, existed mostly in a circularized conformation (Figure 10B), whereas the CS-M mutant, in which the 5′ CS sequence was mutated, was confined to a linear conformation, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by the native PAGE data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The CS-M mutant, in which the 5′ CS sequence was mutated, was confined to a linear conformation.
source: First, using native PAGE, we found that the WT mini-genome, as well as the M1A, M1B, M1C, M3A, M3B, M3C and M2A mini-genomes, existed mostly in a circularized conformation (Figure 10B), whereas the CS-M mutant, in which the 5′ CS sequence was mutated, was confined to a linear conformation, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by the native PAGE data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The M2C mutant mainly stayed in a linear conformation, agreeing with the results of the 5′-3′ RNA binding assay.
source: The M2C mutant also mainly stayed in a linear conformation, agreeing with the results of the 5′-3′ RNA binding assay.
evidence: This is supported by the native PAGE data shown in Figure 10B and is consistent with the RNA binding assay results.

claim: It is unlikely that the UFS duplex structure exists in highly circularized mini-genomes.
source: The above results demonstrated that these corresponding mini-genomes are highly circularized; thus, it is unlikely that the UFS duplex structure exists in them.
evidence: This is inferred from the native PAGE data showing circularized conformation and the SHAPE data showing UFS unwinding during cyclization.

claim: The WT, M1A, M1B and M1C mini-genomes all showed low levels of binding to NS5Pol.
source: Next, the affinity of different mini-genomes for NS5Pol was assessed. The WT, M1A, M1B and M1C mini-genomes all showed low levels of binding to NS5Pol (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The CS-M mini-genome bound to NS5Pol with apparently higher affinity than the other mini-genomes tested.
source: In contrast, the CS-M mini-genome bound to NS5Pol with apparently higher affinity than the other mini-genomes tested (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The CS-M mini-genome showed non-detected or reduced RdRp activity for de novo initiation.
source: Next, an in vitro RdRp assay was performed using mini-genomes as templates. The CS-M mini-genome, together with a mini-genome lacking the SLA element (ΔSLA) or with a disrupted cHP structure (cHP-M), were assayed in parallel as controls, which showed non-detected or reduced RdRp activity for de novo initiation (Figure 10D), in agreement with their known defects in vRNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by the RdRp assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The de novo products in reactions using M1 and M3 series mini-genomes as templates were all reduced compared to those produced using the WT mini-genome as a template.
source: The de novo products in reactions using M1 and M3 series mini-genomes as templates were also all reduced compared to those produced using the WT mini-genome as a template suggesting that the UFS is disabled in mini-genomes because of the unwinding of its duplex (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is supported by the RdRp assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The UFS is disabled in mini-genomes because of the unwinding of its duplex.
source: The de novo products in reactions using M1 and M3 series mini-genomes as templates were also all reduced compared to those produced using the WT mini-genome as a template suggesting that the UFS is disabled in mini-genomes because of the unwinding of its duplex (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is inferred from the RdRp assay data showing reduced activity for UFS mutants in circularized mini-genomes.

claim: The differences in RdRp activity between WT mini-genome and the UFS mutants were likely caused by changes of primary sequence in these constructs.
source: The differences in RdRp activity between WT mini-genome and the UFS mutants were likely caused by changes of primary sequence in these constructs, In supporting of this, the M1C and M3C mutants were not able to reach the same level of replication as WT in replicon assay (Figure 3D), and it has been reported that the base composition of U-rich sequence in the UFS was actually able to affect vRNA replication of DENV2 (Friebe and Harris, 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the RdRp assay data and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Genome cyclization disables the function of the UFS in NS5Pol recruitment.
source: Taken together, the above results demonstrated that genome cyclization disables the function of the UFS in NS5Pol recruitment, suggesting that the UFS has to function dynamically during vRNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the EMSA and RdRp assay data using mini-genomes.

claim: The attenuation of the affinity of NS5Pol for vRNA by genome cyclization is potentially important for the translocation of NS5Pol from the 5′ end to the 3′ end of vRNA.
source: Moreover, the attenuation of the affinity of NS5Pol for vRNA by genome cyclization is potentially important for the translocation of NS5Pol from the 5′ end to the 3′ end of vRNA.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed reduction in NS5Pol binding to circularized genomes.

claim: Both the linear and circular conformations of the flavivirus genome are required for vRNA replication and exist in equilibrium.
source: It has been suggested that both the linear and circular conformations of the flavivirus genome are required for vRNA replication and exist in equilibrium (Villordo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Circular states should be dominant among flavivirus genome conformations.
source: However, circular states should be dominant among its conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from theoretical considerations and experimental observations.

claim: The generic properties of a large RNA molecule lead its two ends to stay close to each other.
source: Although the highly circularized mini-genome is much shorter than the actual viral genome, it has been theoretically proposed that the generic properties of a large RNA molecule lead its two ends to stay close to each other (Yoffe et al., 2011), which was supported by results from single-molecule FRET assays (Leija-Martinez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The 5′ and 3′ ends of the flavivirus genome have great opportunities to contact each other, and due to the high affinity between them, most vRNA molecules would stay circularized in the equilibrium state.
source: Thus, the 5′ and 3′ ends of the flavivirus genome have great opportunities to contact each other, and due to the high affinity between them, most vRNA molecules would stay circularized in the equilibrium state.
evidence: This is inferred from theoretical considerations and experimental observations.

claim: Protein factors have been shown to facilitate the cyclization of mRNA and vRNA in vivo.
source: Moreover, protein factors have been shown to facilitate the cyclization of mRNA and vRNA in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The PABP protein, which bridges mRNA ends through poly(A)-PABP-eIF4E-5′ cap interactions, has been shown to bind to the DENV 3′ UTR.
source: In fact, the PABP protein, which bridges mRNA ends through poly(A)-PABP-eIF4E-5′ cap interactions, has been shown to bind to the DENV 3′ UTR (Polacek et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The UFS duplex is folded during the ongoing synthesis of nascent positive-strand RNA because the 5′ end of the parental (+) strand is released from the dsRNA replication form (RF) by a potential strand-displacement mechanism during the process.
source: Inspired by the co-transcriptional folding of RNA molecules (Frieda and Block, 2012; Gong et al., 2015; Meyer and Miklos, 2004; Perdrizet et al., 2012), we speculated that the UFS duplex is folded during the ongoing synthesis of nascent positive-strand RNA because the 5′ end of the parental (+) strand is released from the dsRNA replication form (RF) by a potential strand-displacement mechanism during the process, given that the flavivirus genus exhibits semi-conservative replication (Chu and Westaway, 1985; Uchil and Satchidanandam, 2003), whereas the 3′ end of the parental (+) strand RNA remains in double-stranded form with the (−) strand.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on co-transcriptional folding principles and supported by citations.

claim: The flavivirus genus exhibits semi-conservative replication.
source: Inspired by the co-transcriptional folding of RNA molecules (Frieda and Block, 2012; Gong et al., 2015; Meyer and Miklos, 2004; Perdrizet et al., 2012), we speculated that the UFS duplex is folded during the ongoing synthesis of nascent positive-strand RNA because the 5′ end of the parental (+) strand is released from the dsRNA replication form (RF) by a potential strand-displacement mechanism during the process, given that the flavivirus genus exhibits semi-conservative replication (Chu and Westaway, 1985; Uchil and Satchidanandam, 2003), whereas the 3′ end of the parental (+) strand RNA remains in double-stranded form with the (−) strand.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The UFS functions as an RNA switch, and its 'ON' and 'OFF' states are controlled by genome cyclization.
source: Based on the above considerations, we proposed that the UFS functions as an RNA switch, and its 'ON' and 'OFF' states are controlled by genome cyclization (Figure 11) to fulfill different needs in vRNA replication.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the combined experimental data.

claim: vRNA released in the cytoplasm is translated to generate a sufficient level of viral proteins, which leads to the eventual binding of NS5 to the SLA and the initiation of (−) strand synthesis, even without the presence of the UFS duplex.
source: A mechanistic model to explain the function of the UFS is described below. (i) vRNA released in the cytoplasm is translated to generate a sufficient level of viral proteins, which leads to the eventual binding of NS5 to the SLA and the initiation of (−) strand synthesis, even without the presence of the UFS duplex.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: Completion of (−) strand synthesis generates the dsRNA RF, which serves as the template for the synthesis of progeny vRNA in the presence of viral NS5/NS3 and other viral/host factors.
source: (ii) Completion of (−) strand synthesis generates the dsRNA RF, which serves as the template for the synthesis of progeny vRNA in the presence of viral NS5/NS3 and other viral/host factors (not shown in Figure 11).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: During the elongation of the nascent (+) strand, the 5′ terminus of the parental (+) strand RNA is displaced first, and the UFS duplex is folded on the protruding 5′ end; this 'ON' state of the UFS facilitates the recruitment of NS5 to the free 5′ end.
source: (iii) During the elongation of the nascent (+) strand, the 5′ terminus of the parental (+) strand RNA is displaced first, and the UFS duplex is folded on the protruding 5′ end; this 'ON' state of the UFS facilitates the recruitment of NS5 to the free 5′ end.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: After the completion of the nascent chain synthesis, the NS5-bound vRNA undergoes genome cyclization, and the UFS element is set to 'OFF' by the hybridization between genome termini, which decreases the binding strength of NS5 to the 5′ terminus and promotes its translocation to the 3′ terminus to initiate next-round synthesis of negative-strand vRNA.
source: (iv) After the completion of the nascent chain synthesis, the NS5-bound vRNA undergoes genome cyclization, and the UFS element is set to 'OFF' by the hybridization between genome termini, which decreases the binding strength of NS5 to the 5′ terminus and promotes its translocation to the 3′ terminus to initiate next-round synthesis of negative-strand vRNA.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: Dynamic modulation of NS5 binding should be of great significance to maintain an appropriate level of (−) vRNA synthesis to ensure the global balance of vRNA replication because the dsRNA RF is a highly active template for (+) vRNA synthesis.
source: Such dynamic modulation of NS5 binding should be of great significance to maintain an appropriate level of (−) vRNA synthesis to ensure the global balance of vRNA replication because the dsRNA RF is a highly active template for (+) vRNA synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional significance of the UFS switching mechanism.

claim: When the terminal secondary structures of both genome conformations of different flaviviruses were examined, the 5′ local structures immediately following the SLA elements were always melted in response to genome cyclization.
source: Furthermore, this RNA-switching mechanism is likely to be universal among flaviviruses with vertebrate hosts given that when the terminal secondary structures of both genome conformations of different flaviviruses were examined, we found that the 5′ local structures immediately following the SLA elements were always melted in response to genome cyclization (Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplements 1–4), suggesting that these structures may possibly possess the same regulatory function as the UFS.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative structural analysis shown in Figure 12 and supplementary figures.

claim: The 5′ local structures immediately following the SLA elements in different flaviviruses may possibly possess the same regulatory function as the UFS.
source: Furthermore, this RNA-switching mechanism is likely to be universal among flaviviruses with vertebrate hosts given that when the terminal secondary structures of both genome conformations of different flaviviruses were examined, we found that the 5′ local structures immediately following the SLA elements were always melted in response to genome cyclization (Figure 12 and Figure 12—figure supplements 1–4), suggesting that these structures may possibly possess the same regulatory function as the UFS.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative structural analysis.

claim: The UFS links two events of vRNA replication, NS5 recruitment and genome cyclization, together.
source: Herein, via the combination of bioinformatics, biochemical and reverse genetics approaches, the UFS element was shown to be crucial for efficient flavivirus vRNA replication through dynamic modulation of viral RdRp recruitment. Our results demonstrated that the UFS links two events of vRNA replication, NS5 recruitment and genome cyclization, together, and the structural stability of the UFS is elaborately balanced to meet the requirements of both.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The structural stability of the UFS is elaborately balanced to meet the requirements of both NS5 recruitment and genome cyclization.
source: Herein, via the combination of bioinformatics, biochemical and reverse genetics approaches, the UFS element was shown to be crucial for efficient flavivirus vRNA replication through dynamic modulation of viral RdRp recruitment. Our results demonstrated that the UFS links two events of vRNA replication, NS5 recruitment and genome cyclization, together, and the structural stability of the UFS is elaborately balanced to meet the requirements of both.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The conformational change of the UFS caused by genome cyclization is coupled with its function in modulating dynamic RdRp recruitment.
source: Especially, the conformational change of the UFS caused by genome cyclization is coupled with its function in modulating dynamic RdRp recruitment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The function of UFS in viral replication and RdRp recruitment was investigated using different flaviviruses (DENV4, JEV and ZIKV).
source: As the function of UFS in viral replication and RdRp recruitment was investigated using different flaviviruses (DENV4, JEV and ZIKV), it is plausible to consider that the UFS is a general regulatory strategy of viral replication among the flavivirus genus.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: It is plausible to consider that the UFS is a general regulatory strategy of viral replication among the flavivirus genus.
source: As the function of UFS in viral replication and RdRp recruitment was investigated using different flaviviruses (DENV4, JEV and ZIKV), it is plausible to consider that the UFS is a general regulatory strategy of viral replication among the flavivirus genus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar UFS function in multiple flaviviruses.

claim: A previous report has suggested that the UFS may not be functional in DENV2.
source: Although a previous report (Filomatori et al., 2011) has suggested that the UFS may not be functional in DENV2, this was more likely to be an exception, as our SHAPE data also indicated that the UFS in DENV2 is highly unstable in vitro, in contrast to the UFS elements from other viruses (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The SHAPE data indicated that the UFS in DENV2 is highly unstable in vitro, in contrast to the UFS elements from other viruses.
source: Although a previous report (Filomatori et al., 2011) has suggested that the UFS may not be functional in DENV2, this was more likely to be an exception, as our SHAPE data also indicated that the UFS in DENV2 is highly unstable in vitro, in contrast to the UFS elements from other viruses (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the SHAPE data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The structure of the downstream SLA region in the 5′ end of the flavivirus genome was unambiguously illuminated by applying a systemic RNA structure prediction and comparison approach covering different members of the flavivirus genus.
source: By applying a systemic RNA structure prediction and comparison approach covering different members of the flavivirus genus, the structure of the downstream SLA region in the 5′ end of the flavivirus genome was unambiguously illuminated.
evidence: This is a summary of the bioinformatics approach used.

claim: The UA-base-pair-rich UFS and the UFS-like element have been identified in MBFVs, two clades of NKVs, and ISFVs, demonstrating that the UFS element is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The UA-base-pair-rich UFS and the UFS-like element have been identified in MBFVs, two clades of NKVs, and ISFVs, demonstrating that the UFS element is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: While the UFS duplex unwinds during genome cyclization in MBFVs and NKVs, neither the conserved mode of genome cyclization nor the unwinding of UFS-like elements during this process was found in ISFVs.
source: Interestingly, while the UFS duplex unwinds during genome cyclization in MBFVs and NKVs, neither the conserved mode of genome cyclization nor the unwinding of UFS-like elements during this process was found in ISFVs.
evidence: This is supported by the structural predictions and comparisons.

claim: The ISFVs have been indicated to be the most divergent outgroup among the genus flavivirus.
source: The ISFVs have been indicated to be the most divergent outgroup among the genus flavivirus (Blitvich and Firth, 2015; Cook and Holmes, 2006; Moureau et al., 2015), which led us to assume that modern flaviviruses are evolved from an insect virus ancestor.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Modern flaviviruses are evolved from an insect virus ancestor.
source: The ISFVs have been indicated to be the most divergent outgroup among the genus flavivirus (Blitvich and Firth, 2015; Cook and Holmes, 2006; Moureau et al., 2015), which led us to assume that modern flaviviruses are evolved from an insect virus ancestor.
